Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England -- A severe rabies epidemic has claimed the lives of at least 83 children within three months in Angola's capital, Luanda, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said. Luanda, which has a large population of stray dogs, also has some of the world's worst slums. Describing the situation as "very worrying,"  WHO rabies expert Francois Meslin told CNN: "This is a huge number and could be the tip of the iceberg." A doctor working at the country's biggest referral hospital Hospital Pediatrico David Bernardino said staff were unable to save any of the children as rabies vaccines had run out. Some of the children were also brought into the hospital too late to be saved, Luis Bernardino, head of the hospital told UN humanitarian organization IRIN. He warned that the number of deaths could be much higher. "The children were brought to our hospital and are the only ones we know of, so the number could be higher," Bernardino told IRIN. "It is a sad moment for us," he added. "I think it was probably that no one was prepared for such a high case load." The number of cases has now started declining, however, said Bernardino. According to Meslin, this could be because the current infected pack of dogs has died. Meslin told CNN that the Angolan government needed to embark on a dog rabies control program urgently to prevent further outbreaks. Angola's capital, where most of the population live in slums, has a large number of stray dogs who are said to have caused the epidemic. "We have had some sporadic cases in other provincial capitals in the country; we think the virus was brought into Luanda and then spread through the dogs -- Angolans love dogs," Bernardino said. "When the first 10 deaths were reported in December 2008 we alerted the authorities, but we do not have veterinary services in the city, no kennels [to keep and observe the animals] and vaccinate them," he added. Another problem contributing to the crisis is that vaccines are too expensive for the average family. "One dose of vaccine costs about $10 and five of those have to be administered, which makes the total cost of treatment $50 which is more than a month's salary for families in most developing countries," Meslin added. In 2008 the WHO wrote that rabies, a disease transmitted from animals with infected saliva to humans, is present on nearly every continent of the world but more that 95 per cent of human deaths occur in Asia and Africa. It can be prevented by vaccination, either prior to exposure or as part of post-exposure treatment. But once symptoms of the disease develop, rabies is fatal. According to the WHO, rabies can affect the lungs, stomach and central nervous systems. In the critical stage, a victim slips into a coma and death, usually due to breathing failure. More than 55,000 people die of rabies each year, the WHO wrote, with 30 to 60 per cent of the victims of dog bites being children under the age of 15.

Luis Bernardino, head of Hospital Pediatrico David Bernardino, Angola’s largest referral hospital, told the UN humanitarian news service IRIN that medical workers could not save any of the children because the hospital had exhausted its supply of rabies vaccine. Bernardino said the actual toll might be considerably greater because hospital officials knew only about the children brought to their facility. Calling it “a sad moment,” he suggested that no one had anticipated such a large number of cases.

The caseload has since begun to fall, Bernardino said. Meslin explained that one possible reason was that the group of infected dogs responsible for the outbreak had died. He urged Angola’s government to establish an immediate canine rabies-control campaign to stop similar epidemics from occurring again.

Stray dogs, which are numerous in Luanda, are believed to have driven the outbreak. Most residents of the capital live in slum areas. Bernardino said isolated cases had previously appeared in other provincial capitals, and officials believed the virus was introduced into Luanda before spreading among dogs, which are popular pets among Angolans.

Authorities were notified after the first 10 deaths were recorded in December 2008, Bernardino said. However, Luanda lacked veterinary services and had no kennels where animals could be confined, monitored and vaccinated.

The price of vaccination has also worsened the emergency because treatment is beyond the means of many ordinary families. Meslin said each vaccine dose costs approximately $10, while the full treatment requires five doses. The resulting $50 expense exceeds a month’s income for families in many developing nations.

In 2008, the WHO reported that rabies occurs on almost every continent, although more than 95 percent of human fatalities are in Africa and Asia. The disease passes to people through the infected saliva of animals. It can be prevented through vaccination before exposure or through treatment administered afterward. Once symptoms appear, however, the infection is fatal.

According to the WHO, rabies may affect the lungs, stomach and central nervous system. During its most severe phase, patients enter a coma and die, most often from respiratory failure.

The WHO estimates that rabies causes more than 55,000 deaths annually. Children younger than 15 account for between 30 and 60 percent of dog-bite victims.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed newspaper article on Angola’s 2008–2009 rabies outbreak, explaining the role of stray dogs, vaccine shortages, treatment costs, weak veterinary services, and the impact on children.
counterfactuals.output:
# Stray Dogs, Scarce Vaccines: How Rabies Took a Deadly Toll on Angola’s Children

**LUANDA, Angola —** In the crowded neighborhoods of Angola’s capital, dogs roam between open-air markets, rubbish heaps and unpaved streets. Many have no identifiable owner. Few have been vaccinated. During 2008 and 2009, that combination helped turn a preventable disease into a deadly public-health emergency.

By May 2009, health authorities had recorded **at least 93 human rabies deaths in Luanda since the beginning of the year**, according to figures reported by the World Health Organization. Most of the victims were children. Additional deaths had been reported in 2008, and officials feared the true toll was higher because some families never reached a hospital or sought care only after symptoms had begun.

The outbreak exposed weaknesses at nearly every point in Angola’s defenses against rabies: uncontrolled dog populations, limited veterinary coverage, shortages of human and animal vaccines, expensive treatment after bites, inadequate public awareness and an overburdened health system still recovering from decades of civil war.

Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is almost invariably fatal. Yet timely post-exposure treatment can prevent the disease. In Angola, the distance between those two facts was measured in money, vaccine supplies and access to care.

## Children at greatest risk

Children accounted for the majority of reported deaths, especially those under 15. Their vulnerability was not accidental.

Young children are more likely to play near dogs, to approach unfamiliar animals and to suffer bites to the face, head or upper body. Those wounds can allow the virus to reach the brain more rapidly than bites to the legs. Children may also fail to tell adults that they have been bitten or scratched, particularly when the injury appears small.

In Luanda’s densely populated outskirts, the risk was intensified by daily contact between children and free-roaming dogs. Waste collection was irregular in many areas, leaving food scraps that sustained packs of animals. Dogs moved easily between homes, streets and markets, blurring the line between owned animals and strays.

Some families washed bite wounds or turned to traditional remedies but did not immediately seek medical care. Others traveled from one clinic to another looking for vaccine. By the time fever, agitation, difficulty swallowing, paralysis or fear of water appeared, doctors could offer little beyond supportive care.

Rabies can incubate for weeks or months, giving families a deceptive period in which an injured child appears healthy. That delay sometimes encouraged parents to believe the danger had passed.

## Stray dogs at the center of transmission

Domestic dogs were the principal source of human infection. Angola’s outbreak was not driven mainly by wild animals but by an urban cycle in which infected dogs bit people and other dogs.

The term “stray” concealed a complicated reality. Some animals were genuinely ownerless. Others belonged loosely to households but were allowed to roam, were rarely examined by veterinarians and had never received a rabies vaccine. Owners often lacked vaccination certificates or did not know whether an animal’s protection was current.

Weak control of dog breeding added to the problem. Puppies were born faster than municipal authorities could register, vaccinate or remove them. Abandoned animals joined roaming packs, while inadequate rubbish disposal provided a continuing source of food.

Authorities responded with emergency dog-vaccination campaigns and, in some areas, the capture or killing of free-roaming animals. Such measures could reduce immediate danger, but public-health specialists emphasized that indiscriminate culling alone would not stop rabies. Dog populations can quickly rebound unless campaigns achieve broad, repeated vaccination coverage and are combined with registration, sterilization, waste management and responsible ownership.

Experts generally regard vaccination of at least about 70 percent of the dog population as the most effective way to interrupt canine rabies transmission. Reaching that level requires reliable estimates of dog numbers, trained teams, cold-storage equipment, transport and sustained community participation—all difficult to secure in rapidly expanding settlements.

## Human vaccine supplies fell short

For a person bitten by a potentially rabid animal, the first steps should be immediate and thorough washing of the wound with soap and running water, application of an antiseptic if available, and prompt medical assessment.

Depending on previous vaccination and the severity of the exposure, patients may need a full course of rabies vaccine. Severe bites—especially those that break the skin or involve saliva contacting mucous membranes—may also require **rabies immunoglobulin**, which provides immediate antibodies while the vaccine stimulates the patient’s own immune response.

During the Angolan emergency, access to these products was uneven. Clinics reported shortages, and supplies were concentrated in a limited number of facilities. Rabies immunoglobulin was particularly difficult to obtain because it is more expensive and requires careful storage and administration.

Even when vaccine was available, patients had to return for several doses over a period of weeks. For poor families, each visit could mean transport fares, missed work, long queues and the possibility of being told that supplies had run out. A child might receive the first injection but fail to complete the course.

Emergency shipments and vaccination campaigns helped ease some shortages, but they did not resolve the underlying problem: Angola lacked a consistently financed and distributed stock of post-exposure treatment sufficient for the number of bites occurring in and around Luanda.

## The high price of survival

The cost of post-exposure treatment placed protection beyond the reach of some families, particularly when vaccine or immunoglobulin had to be obtained outside the public system.

Internationally procured vaccine courses could cost many tens of dollars, while a complete regimen including immunoglobulin could rise to well over $100, depending on the product, the patient’s weight and where it was purchased. In Angola, where many households survived on low and irregular incomes, even transport and consultation costs could force families to delay care.

The economic burden did not end with the medicine. Parents often lost wages while taking children to repeated appointments. Families arriving from distant districts had to pay for travel and sometimes accommodation. If a clinic lacked vaccine, they might have to visit several hospitals or pharmacies.

That made rabies a disease shaped by inequality. Families with money, transport and information had a better chance of obtaining prompt treatment. Those living in informal settlements or outside the capital were more likely to encounter delays at every stage.

## Veterinary services struggled to keep pace

The outbreak also revealed the weakness of Angola’s veterinary network. The country’s long civil war ended in 2002, but the conflict had damaged infrastructure and displaced millions of people. Rapid migration into Luanda then expanded the city faster than sanitation, animal-control and health services could develop.

Veterinary departments lacked enough staff, vehicles and vaccine to conduct routine mass immunization. Surveillance was fragmented, making it difficult to determine how many dogs were infected, where transmission was accelerating or whether vaccination campaigns had reached enough animals.

Laboratory capacity was limited, and not every suspected animal could be tested. Dogs that bit people sometimes disappeared or were killed and discarded before they could be observed or examined. Without reliable animal surveillance, health workers often had to treat bites as potential rabies exposures without knowing whether the dog had been infected.

Coordination between hospitals, veterinary authorities, municipal governments and waste-management services was also inconsistent. Human-health officials might record a bite or death without rapidly triggering an investigation in the neighborhood where the attack occurred. Veterinary teams, in turn, might not have the resources to vaccinate surrounding dogs.

Rabies control depends on precisely that kind of cooperation. The disease moves between animals and people, so treating human victims without controlling infection in dogs can only limit the damage, not end transmission.

## Fear spread with the disease

Reports of children dying after dog bites caused alarm across Luanda. Families became wary of animals that had previously been accepted as part of neighborhood life. Schools and public-information campaigns warned children not to touch unfamiliar dogs and urged parents to seek care immediately after a bite.

But messages about prevention competed with confusion. Some residents believed that only visibly aggressive or foaming dogs could transmit the virus. In reality, infected animals can be contagious before the most recognizable signs appear. Scratches and saliva exposure may also carry risk, not only dramatic bites.

Public fear sometimes led residents to kill dogs indiscriminately. Health specialists warned that poorly organized culling could scatter animal populations and make vaccination harder. It also risked removing vaccinated or confined dogs while failing to reach the roaming animals most likely to transmit disease.

## A preventable emergency

Angola’s 2008–2009 outbreak was especially tragic because the essential tools to prevent rabies were already known.

Routine vaccination of dogs can stop transmission at its source. Immediate wound cleaning sharply reduces risk. Prompt vaccine, combined with immunoglobulin for serious exposures, can prevent death even after a bite. Public education can help children avoid dangerous animals and encourage families to report injuries quickly.

What Angola lacked was not scientific knowledge but dependable delivery.

The crisis prompted emergency vaccination efforts, greater public awareness and international assistance. Yet specialists cautioned that short campaigns would not be enough. Dog vaccination must be repeated regularly as new animals are born. Clinics need permanent stocks of human vaccine and immunoglobulin. Veterinary surveillance must extend beyond central Luanda into peri-urban and rural districts. Bite cases must be reported quickly and linked to investigations of the animal involved.

Improved rubbish collection, dog registration, sterilization programs and enforcement of responsible ownership are also part of rabies prevention. Without them, the ecological conditions that sustained large numbers of roaming dogs would remain.

For Angola’s children, the stakes were immediate. A momentary encounter on the way to school or while playing outside could lead to weeks of searching for treatment—and, if treatment came too late, an agonizing death.

The outbreak demonstrated a harsh public-health lesson: rabies rarely kills because medicine has no answer. It kills when vaccination does not reach dogs, when treatment does not reach bite victims and when poverty turns a preventable exposure into a fatal one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the WHO’s warning about a severe rabies crisis in Luanda. Include the death toll, quotations from health officials, possible reasons cases are declining, and global rabies statistics.
counterfactuals.output:
## WHO warns of severe rabies crisis in Luanda

The World Health Organization has described rabies in Angola’s capital, Luanda, as a **“severe public-health crisis.”** According to figures released for the first four months of 2025, **54 people died between January and April**, many of them children, after exposure—usually bites—to infected dogs.

WHO’s representative in Angola, **Dr. Indrajit Hazarika**, stressed that **“rabies is 100% preventable”** when bite victims promptly receive wound care, rabies vaccine and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin. Health officials said the deaths were especially troubling because treatment after exposure can prevent the disease, whereas rabies is almost invariably fatal once symptoms appear.

Reported deaths declined month by month during the period. Officials said possible explanations included:

- greater public awareness and faster reporting after dog bites;
- improved access to post-exposure vaccination;
- vaccination and control campaigns targeting dogs;
- closer coordination between human- and animal-health services.

They cautioned, however, that the decline was not yet proof that the crisis had been brought under control. Luanda’s large population of unvaccinated and stray dogs, gaps in vaccine availability, and delays in seeking treatment remain major risks.

### Global context

WHO estimates that rabies causes about **59,000 human deaths worldwide each year**. Approximately **95% occur in Africa and Asia**, and **children under 15 account for about 40% of people bitten by animals suspected of carrying rabies**. Dogs are responsible for **up to 99% of human rabies transmission**.

WHO and its partners aim to eliminate human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by **2030**, chiefly through mass dog vaccination, reliable access to post-exposure treatment and public education.

**LONDON —** More than 90 children have died from rabies in Angola’s capital after being bitten by infected dogs, according to information reported by the World Health Organization and cited by CNN and the U.N. humanitarian news service IRIN.

The deaths, reported in Luanda during the first months of 2009, prompted Angolan authorities and international health agencies to intensify dog-vaccination efforts and improve access to emergency treatment for bite victims. Children were particularly vulnerable because they were more likely to be bitten and less likely to report an injury quickly.

Rabies is a viral disease transmitted through the saliva of infected mammals, most commonly through a bite or scratch from a dog. It can be prevented if treatment begins promptly. The WHO recommends immediately washing the wound thoroughly with soap and water, followed by a course of rabies vaccine and, for severe exposures, rabies immunoglobulin.

Once symptoms appear, however, rabies is virtually always fatal. Early signs can include fever, headache, weakness and pain or tingling at the bite site. The disease then attacks the nervous system, causing agitation, hallucinations, difficulty swallowing, fear of water, paralysis, coma and death.

Health officials have emphasized that vaccinating dogs is the most effective way to stop human rabies deaths. Angola’s outbreak was linked to large numbers of unvaccinated and stray dogs, while shortages of vaccine, delayed treatment and limited public awareness increased the danger to children.

Authorities urged anyone bitten or scratched by a potentially infected animal to clean the wound immediately and seek medical care without waiting for symptoms.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an article explaining why dozens of children in Angola’s capital died from rabies despite the disease being preventable, focusing on poverty, overcrowded slums, stray dogs, delayed hospital treatment, and the high cost and limited supply of vaccines.
counterfactuals.output:
# Why Preventable Rabies Is Killing Children in Angola’s Capital

Rabies is among the world’s most preventable infectious diseases. A prompt course of vaccination after a dog bite can stop the virus before it reaches the brain, while vaccinating dogs can prevent transmission in the first place. Yet dozens of children in Luanda, Angola’s capital, have died from the disease—a tragedy driven less by medical uncertainty than by poverty, overcrowding and failures in access to basic health care.

In Luanda’s densely populated informal settlements, many families live among large numbers of unvaccinated and ownerless dogs. Poor waste collection leaves food scraps in streets and open dumps, allowing stray dog populations to grow. Children are particularly exposed because they often play outdoors, may approach animals and are more likely to suffer bites to the face or upper body, which can allow the virus to reach the brain more quickly.

Controlling rabies requires widespread dog vaccination, management of stray populations and public education. But these measures are difficult to sustain in fast-growing neighborhoods where sanitation, housing and health services are already under pressure. Many dogs have never been vaccinated, and an animal that bites a child may disappear before it can be observed or tested.

The danger is often compounded by delayed treatment. A bite may initially appear minor, and parents may not understand that even a small scratch or contact between infected saliva and broken skin can transmit rabies. Some families first clean the wound at home or seek traditional remedies. Others wait because reaching a hospital means paying for transport, missing work or spending hours at an overcrowded facility.

These delays can be fatal. The wound should be washed immediately and thoroughly with soap and running water, and the patient should receive post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible. This usually includes a series of rabies vaccine doses. For severe exposures, rabies immunoglobulin or an equivalent antibody treatment is also needed around the wound.

In Luanda, however, the necessary products can be scarce. Public hospitals may run out, forcing families to search from clinic to clinic or turn to private pharmacies. When vaccines are available commercially, their price can be far beyond the means of households already struggling to pay for food and shelter. Because treatment requires multiple doses, the total cost includes not only the medicine but repeated transport and lost income. Limited supplies of rabies immunoglobulin create an additional barrier for children with serious bites.

Once symptoms begin—often with fever, pain or tingling at the bite site, followed by agitation, difficulty swallowing, fear of water or paralysis—rabies is almost always fatal. At that point, hospital care can generally provide only comfort. This grim reality means every missed or delayed vaccine represents a race the virus may win.

The deaths in Luanda therefore reflect a chain of preventable failures: too many unvaccinated stray dogs, unsafe and overcrowded living conditions, inadequate public awareness, delayed access to hospitals, and vaccines that are either unavailable or unaffordable. Poor children bear the greatest risk because they are more exposed to dogs and their families have the fewest resources to obtain urgent treatment.

Preventing further deaths requires more than emergency supplies during an outbreak. Authorities need reliable stocks of free post-exposure vaccines and antibody treatments, available close to high-risk communities. Health workers must be trained to assess bites and begin treatment immediately. Public campaigns should teach families to wash wounds, report bites and seek medical care without delay.

Most importantly, Angola must reduce the disease at its source through sustained mass vaccination of dogs, better waste management, responsible ownership and humane control of stray populations. Rabies deaths are not inevitable. When children die from the disease, it is a sign that proven protections failed to reach the people who needed them most.
